items.abstract: The Sudanese Middle Stone Age (MSA) represents a crucial context for understanding human dispersal, technological innovation, and cultural adaptation during the late Pleistocene. Yet, after nearly a century of Pleistocene archaeology in Sudan, no standardized database of this record has existed. Research in this area has long been characterized by the diverse and fragmented nature of individual studies, resulting in incomplete datasets, variable chronological control, and limited comparability across the published record. The Sudan MSA Lithic and Contextual Database (SUM) presents a clean, standardized dataset of 283 sites that integrates geographic location, chronological setting, environmental context, raw material availability, and technological strategies to address these challenges. Through a critical assessment of available data and the application of a controlled glossary of terms, SUM ensures comparability and provides a reliable basis for synthesis. Preliminary results demonstrate the wide distribution of Levallois and Nubian Levallois technologies in Sudan, but also reveal large chronological gaps, as only 17 out of 283 sites have yielded absolute dates. SUM thus represents the first comprehensive and standardized dataset for the Sudanese MSA and constitutes an important resource for future research on technological diversity, ecological adaptation, and human dispersal.

items.title: The Sudan Middle Stone Age Lithic and Contextual Database (SUM): Structure, Research Potential, and Future Directions

items.abstract: Abstract Whether the last common ancestor (LCA) of Homo and Pan ( ca. 6–7 Ma) used stone tools is a foundational question in palaeoanthropology. However, it is often treated as known rather than as a hypothesis requiring substantiation. Lacking fossil evidence for the LCA, this assumption is based on data from extant primates and the available hominin fossil record. Phylogenetic approaches invoking parsimony argue that the presence of stone tool use in both Pan and Homo reflects homology rather than convergent evolution. While methodologically legitimate, we argue that this framework has been applied without sufficient attention to the specific criteria for this to be true. For homology to hold, stone tool use must have been continuously expressed across generations of both lineages from the LCA to the present. We evaluate this claim against three lines of evidence: behavioural data from extant primates, showing that stone tool use is heterogeneous within Pan ; the hominin fossil and archaeological record, which leaves a substantial evidential gap between the LCA and the earliest known documented technologies; and comparative data from phylogenetically distant tool using animals, which show that similar behaviours can arise independently under comparable ecological conditions. Together, these lines of evidence favour a model of multiple, context-dependent origins of stone tool use over unbroken inheritance from a tool using LCA.
